name: South Calumet
description:
South Calumet is where the old world died loudest. When U.S. Steel, Republic Steel, and Wisconsin Steel were running three shifts a day, the far Southeast Side was the muscle of a city that built things — actual, physical things made of iron and carbon and labor. The Calumet River carried ore and slag. The air tasted like metal. The work was brutal and the pay was enough. Then the mills closed, one by one, and the neighborhood learned what every industrial community learns: the company needed you, until it didn't. South Calumet was already a ruin before the collapse. The collapse just made it official.

What Axiom Industries found when it surveyed the far Southeast Side was a ready-made industrial zone — brownfield sites, deepwater river access, existing heavy infrastructure, and a population too small and too low-tier to resist rezoning. Axiom reactivated the Calumet River corridor as a Tier 1 industrial processing zone, running automated recycling and material reclamation operations in the shells of the old steel mills. The mills that once employed thousands now employ dozens — human oversight for robotic systems that strip, sort, and reprocess the material output of Meridian's consumption. The work is toxic, monotonous, and pays just enough to keep a Tier 1 credential active. The workers call themselves steelgrave diggers, because they're mining the corpse of the industry that made this place.

The residential community clings to the edges of the industrial zone like moss on a factory wall. Housing is dense, low-rise, and located downwind of operations that Axiom's environmental reports describe as within acceptable parameters. The acceptable parameters are set by Axiom. Lake Michigan is visible from the eastern blocks, but the shoreline is restricted — Axiom controls waterfront access for cargo operations. The Calumet River, once the neighborhood's economic artery, is now a corporate logistics channel: automated barges moving reclaimed materials to processing facilities further north. Residents can see the river. They cannot reach it without crossing corporate sovereign territory.

But South Calumet has a resource that Axiom's surveys didn't account for: institutional memory. The union halls are still standing. The organizing traditions that built the labor movement in this part of the city didn't disappear when the mills closed — they went dormant. The steelgrave diggers have started talking in the old vocabulary: collective bargaining, work actions, solidarity. It's small, it's quiet, and it's the first labor organizing in Axiom's industrial zones in over a decade. If it succeeds, the implications extend far beyond one district. If it's discovered, the implications for the organizers will be personal and severe.

sights: Automated recycling operations in the skeletal frames of old steel mills — robots working where thousands once stood
The Calumet River choked with automated barges, moving in formation, navigation lights reflecting off dark water
Residential blocks huddled against the industrial zone perimeter, laundry lines strung between buildings like flags of occupation
Lake Michigan visible between industrial structures — a glimpse of open water you can't reach
The old union hall, its facade weathered but intact, lights on inside after shift change
Smokestacks that haven't produced smoke in decades standing like headstones over the industrial zone
sounds: The grinding rhythm of automated material reclamation — metal on metal, continuous, the district's heartbeat
Barge navigation signals on the Calumet River, mechanical and regular
Wind off the lake hitting the industrial structures, producing a low moan that residents stop hearing after the first year
Shift-change announcements from Axiom's facility speakers, audible in the residential blocks whether they want to hear them or not
Quiet conversations in the union hall after hours, voices kept low out of habit and necessity
smells: Metal and chemical processing — a taste more than a smell, coating the back of the throat
River water carrying industrial runoff, a particular stink that South Calumet natives identify as home
Lake air when the wind shifts east, briefly clean, a reminder of what air could be
Machine oil and recycled lubricant from the automated facilities, drifting into the residential blocks
atmosphere.feel: South Calumet feels like a place that has been used up and is being used again. The exhaustion is in the buildings, the soil, the water, the people. But there's something under the exhaustion — a stubbornness inherited from the union era, a refusal to accept that labor has no leverage. The feeling is pre-storm: everything is quiet and everything is charged.

demographics: Approximately 15,000 residents, down from 40,000 in the steel era. Mixed-heritage community — historically Eastern European and Mexican-American, now joined by climate refugees and displaced workers from other collapsed industrial zones. Predominantly Tier 1. The population is aging and the young leave when they can.
economy: Axiom automated recycling and material reclamation. Subsistence wages for human oversight positions. Small-scale fishing on restricted lake access. An informal economy of repair and salvage that operates in the margins of the industrial zone.
power_structure: Axiom Industries holds sovereign authority over the industrial zone and waterfront. Residential blocks fall under general Axiom governance with minimal services. The nascent labor organizing in the union hall represents the only challenge to Axiom's authority, and it hasn't revealed itself yet.
dangers: Toxic exposure from industrial operations — respiratory and neurological effects are documented by community clinicians and ignored by Axiom
Axiom security monitors the industrial zone perimeter and treats unauthorized access as trespassing in sovereign territory
Labor organizing, if discovered, will be met with termination, tier demotion, and possible relocation to lower-tier zones
The Calumet River's automated barge traffic is hazardous to anyone in the water — the systems don't detect human-sized objects
Structural decay in the residential blocks, where Axiom has no maintenance obligation and the residents have no maintenance budget
opportunities: The union hall's organizing effort, if supported, could become the first successful collective action against Axiom's industrial operations
Axiom's automated systems have documented vulnerabilities — the recycling facilities run on legacy software that hasn't been updated
The Calumet River provides water access to the broader southern waterway network, if you can navigate the barge traffic
Institutional memory of labor organizing tactics is a strategic resource that other districts lack
Environmental data from South Calumet could support legal challenges to Axiom's industrial operations across Meridian
story_hooks: The steelgrave diggers' organizing effort has been infiltrated — someone in the union hall meetings is reporting to Axiom. The organizers need to identify the informant before their next action, planned for the month's end.

An automated recycling facility has uncovered something in the material stream that wasn't supposed to be there — pre-collapse military hardware, still functional, mixed into a shipment of reclaimed construction materials. Axiom doesn't know yet. The shift supervisor who found it has forty-eight hours before the next inventory audit.

A retired steelworker from the original mills has been mapping the underground infrastructure beneath the industrial zone — tunnels, pipes, access points that predate Axiom's occupation. He's offering the maps to anyone who'll promise to use them.
frequented_by: Steelgrave diggers — Axiom's human oversight workers, tired and getting organized
Union hall regulars maintaining traditions that predate the corporate era
River runners using the Calumet's waterways for unauthorized transport
Axiom logistics personnel managing the automated operations from climate-controlled offices they never leave
Community clinicians documenting health impacts that official records don't acknowledge
